## Automated AI review

> **Community review:** Independent automated community review, unaffiliated with the Omarchy team, intended to help prepare PRs for their review.

**Verified:** the new wait loop fixes the reported case, a shell that exits cleanly but takes longer than the 5 s kill timeout. Two issues remain on the new SIGKILL path: the old shell's supervisor relaunches it, and the PID passed to `kill -KILL` is not validated.

| Old shell exits cleanly about 7 s after the kill request (synthetic Quickshell, production scripts) | restart exit | live shells afterwards |
|---|---|---|
| base | 0 | **0** (fresh `-n` refused as a duplicate) |
| head | 0 | **1** |

**Verified:**
- `jq -r '.[]?.pid'` matches the Quickshell v0.3.1 `list -j` output: a JSON array of objects with a numeric `pid`, or plain text when no instance is running.
- The loop waits on the same instance-lock liveness that `quickshell -n` uses for its duplicate check.
- The PR's test passes all 8 cases on head. On base the new case fails at `restart forces a shell that will not exit`, as the description states.

### A force-killed shell is relaunched by its old supervisor

In a session the shell runs under `omarchy-launch-shell`. That launcher treats exit status 137 as a crash and runs `quickshell -n` again after a 1 s backoff. Nothing tells it that the SIGKILL came from a restart. Meanwhile the restart has already dispatched a fresh launcher. Quickshell's `-n` duplicate check is not atomic with lock creation: `launch.cpp` creates the instance lock only after GUI and plugin initialization. So the two launchers race.

Timeline from a synthetic Quickshell, driven by the production head `omarchy-restart-shell` and `omarchy-launch-shell`. Times are relative to the old supervisor's "status 137; relaunching" log line. The startup delays are chosen parameters, not measurements.

```text
                                    0.2 s startup       1.2 s startup
restart dispatches new launcher     +0.11 s             +0.11 s
new instance passes -n check        +0.12 s             +0.12 s
new instance creates its lock       +0.33 s             +1.33 s
old supervisor's -n relaunch        +1.01 s  refused    +1.01 s  passes (no lock yet)
live shells afterwards              1                   2
restart exit                        0                   0
```

**Impact:** this affects only the escalation the PR adds, a shell still alive about 9-10 s into the restart. With a fast startup the only effect is a misleading crash-style journal entry. If startup between the check and the lock takes longer than about 0.9 s, two shells run the same config, and the restart still reports success: its readiness ping only checks that some shell answers. How long real Quickshell takes at that point was not measured. A third ordering is possible by source: the old supervisor wins, the fresh launcher is refused, and the shell keeps running under the old supervisor.

**Suggested change:** stop the old supervisor before forcing its shell. Its `stop` trap handles SIGTERM, forwards it to the shell and exits without relaunching. So SIGTERM the verified `omarchy-launch-shell` parent of a lingering PID first, and keep SIGKILL for whatever remains. A restart marker that the launcher checks before relaunching would also work. Keep relaunching after unrelated crashes. A diagnostic copy of the restart script that adds this SIGTERM step removed the relaunch at both startup delays and still passes the PR's test. Trade-off: in the 10 s give-up path, the old supervisor no longer brings a shell back on its own.

**Optional test improvement:** the new test's stubborn shell is a bare `sleep`, not a child of `omarchy-launch-shell`, and its assertions run before the launcher's 1 s backoff ends. In the synthetic runs, running the real launcher as its supervisor and counting launches after the backoff exposed the extra relaunch.

### An unreadable instance record turns into `kill -KILL 0`

`quickshell list` decides an instance is live from its lock, then prints the `pid` stored inside the lock file. It never checks whether reading that data succeeded (`paths.cpp` `checkLock`/`collectInstances`, `command.cpp` `listInstances`). With Qt 6.11.2, a short read leaves the value at 0. Two conditions can produce such a record for a live shell:
- A lock that was taken but whose data was never fully written. `createLock` takes the lock before writing and does not check the write.
- A shell started by Quickshell 0.2.1 that is still running after an upgrade to 0.3.x. The 0.3.x reader expects two extra fields, and the `pid` read runs past the end of the old record.

```text
list -j  ->  [{"pid": 0, ...}]  ->  lingering=(0)  ->  after grace: kill -KILL 0
                                                        = SIGKILL to the restart's own process group
```

**Impact:** `kill -KILL 0` signals every process in the caller's process group. The restart dies with status 137 and no message, and the old shell is left running with no replacement. When the restart runs from `omarchy-update` through `omarchy-update-restart`, that group normally includes the update job itself. The upgrade case also needs the old shell to still be alive after the grace period. Base never passed a PID from `list` to `kill`, so this exposure is new in this PR. It was established from Quickshell and Qt source and was not executed.

**Suggested change:** validate each PID before signalling it, while still counting every listed instance so the loop keeps waiting and the 10 s give-up message still applies:

```bash
if (( SECONDS >= grace_deadline )); then
  for pid in "${lingering[@]}"; do
    [[ $pid =~ ^[1-9][0-9]*$ ]] && (( pid != $$ )) && kill -KILL "$pid" 2>/dev/null
  done
fi
```

Optionally, also confirm the target is a Quickshell process before forcing it.

**Note:** the comment kept above the kill loop still says the loop "can't race a dying shell". The new comment directly below it explains that it can.
